extracted.intended_audience: writers seeking information about literary agents; general readers interested in publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of what a literary agent does and the common criteria used to identify legitimate or appropriate agents (fees, specialties, size, membership/ethics, role in the publishing process). Useful for authors seeking representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary agent is an agent who represents writers and their written works to publishers, theatrical producers, film producers, and film studios, and assists in sale and deal negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most often represent novelists, screenwriters, and non-fiction writers. This explains the principal functions an agent performs (representation to publishers/productions and negotiation of sales/deals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of authors/genres represented
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary agencies can range in size ... Most agencies, especially smaller ones, specialize to some degree. They may represent—for example—authors of science fiction, mainstream thrillers and mysteries, children's books, romance, or highly topical nonfiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should look for agents who specialize in their genre; note that very few agents represent short stories or poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and commission practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputable literary agents generally charge a commission and do not charge a fee upfront. The commission rate is generally 15%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A red flag is an agent demanding upfront fees; standard practice is to take a percentage of sales (commonly ~15%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency size and internal specializations
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary agencies can range in size from a single agent who represents perhaps a dozen authors, to a substantial firm with senior partners, sub-agents, specialists in areas like foreign rights or licensed merchandise tie-ins, and clients numbering in the hundreds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The size of an agency affects resources and available specialist support (e.g., foreign rights, merchandising); authors should consider whether a large firm or a solo agent better fits their needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and professional association membership (AAR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimate agents and agencies in the book world are not required to be members of the Association of Authors' Representatives (AAR), but according to Writer's Market listings, many agents in the United States are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify for AAR membership, agents must have sold a minimum number of books and pledge to abide by a Canon of Ethics. AAR membership can be a signal of experience and an ethical commitment, but absence of membership is not definitive proof of illegitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent's role in the broader publishing workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: In the book publishing process, the literary agent sits between submission and the publisher's reader/contract negotiation, connecting authors with publishers and participating in contract negotiation, rights and royalty discussions, and other deal terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agent's responsibilities include presenting submissions, negotiating contracts (intellectual property rights, royalty rates, format, etc.), and often coordinating with editors, copy editors, and other production roles described in the publishing chain.
